resident.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old man presented with neck pain of 6 months' duration, with paraesthesia radiating from both shoulders to the fingers, and worsening weakness in both lower extremities over 5 months.
resident.history: The patient had intermittent neck pain with paraesthesia in both shoulders radiating to the fingers, mostly during activities, for 6 months. There was no prior trauma. Over the following 5 months, the pain and paraesthesia worsened, and he developed weakness in both lower extremities. He consulted a neurosurgeon, who stated there was nerve entrapment. He underwent physiotherapy for 4 months without improvement. He then presented to our hospital. He worked as a contractor and mostly sat behind a desk. He denied any decrease in body weight or appetite and had no history of chronic cough.
resident.physical_exam: On physical examination, general condition was unremarkable (further details not documented). There was no tenderness on palpation along the midline. Examination of the cervical spine showed positive Lhermitte test, finger-escape test, grip-and-release test, Hoffman-Tromner sign, and Spurling sign. The patient was able to move his neck normally. Further examination revealed diminished motoric strength in all extremities with positive Babinski reflex and clonus, with normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes. He had urinary retention and faecal incontinence. Radiographic examination showed straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter of 10 mm and a Torg ratio of 0.37. There was osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 levels with spur formation at C3 through C5. Magnetic resonance imaging showed cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 levels and spinal cord compression. Laboratory findings were unremarkable except for leukocytosis.
key_positive_signs: Diminished motor strength in all extremities
Radiographic straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter 10 mm and Torg ratio 0.37
Osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 with spur formation at C3-C5
MRI cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 with spinal cord compression

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy, plus a likely cervical radiculopathy (C5 or C6) suggested by radicular symptoms and a positive Spurling sign.

red_flags.finding: Positive Spurling sign with paresthesias radiating from shoulders to fingers
red_flags.rationale: Indicates a radicular component in addition to myelopathy. The MRI report describes canal stenosis and cord compression but does not mention foraminal stenosis; if present, decompression should address the nerve roots as well.

red_flags.finding: Normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes despite positive Babinski reflex and clonus
red_flags.rationale: Upper motor neuron lesions typically cause hyperreflexia. Normal DTRs may reflect early myelopathy or a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, but they do not undermine the evidence of cord compression.
Not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of the myelopathy. It may indicate an unrelated infection or inflammation but does not alter the localization or indication.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The MRI report describes central canal stenosis and cord compression at C4-C5, which explains the myelopathic syndrome. However, the radicular symptoms (shoulder-to-finger paresthesias, positive Spurling sign) are not directly explained by the reported imaging; foraminal stenosis is not described.
neurology.public_message: Localization: cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy; additional radicular component suggested by Spurling sign and radiating paresthesias. Imaging-symptom match is high for the dominant myelopathic syndrome. Red flags: (1) Positive Spurling sign with radicular symptoms—changes_plan—may indicate foraminal stenosis requiring decompression of nerve roots; MRI did not describe foramina. (2) Normal patellar and Achilles reflexes despite Babinski and clonus—coexisting—an atypical finding possibly due to early myelopathy or coexisting peripheral neuropathy; does not alter the main diagnosis. (3) Leukocytosis—coexisting—incidental laboratory abnormality not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of cord compression.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III; intraoperative MAP target 85 mmHg; blood loss risk low; prone position tolerance moderate; extubation difficulty unassessable because no airway assessment is documented.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or worsening of myelopathic symptoms (gait, strength, bladder/bowel function) after 6 weeks of structured conservative care.
Progression of neurological deficits on serial examination.
New or worsening cord signal change on MRI.
Development of acute urinary retention or faecal incontinence (already present; if worsens).
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the progressive myelopathy and the evidence that delay may risk irreversible cord damage. However, the patient is only 50 years old and has not had a structured, supervised conservative program with clear goals and close monitoring. I propose a formal 3-6 month course of intensive physical therapy, core strengthening, posture management, and symptom control, with defined failure criteria. Success rates from structured conservative care in mild-to-moderate compressive myelopathy are around 30%, but in this case with severe myelopathy and already failed physiotherapy, that figure may be optimistic. Nevertheless, given the risks of surgery, a time-limited trial under strict supervision is a reasonable first step. If there is no improvement after 6 weeks or if neurological deficits worsen, I would accept surgery.

preconditions_for_failure: Sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention and faecal incontinence) fails to improve or worsens under conservative care
Progressive myelopathy (documented weakness, hyperreflexia, Babinski, clonus) despite 4 months of physiotherapy
Cord compression at C4-C5 with clinical myelopathy and risk of irreversible cord damage
persuaded_by: Sphincter dysfunction combined with progressive myelopathy and cord compression at C4-C5 indicates a high risk of irreversible spinal cord injury; this specific combination was underweighted in my initial proposal and makes further conservative care unsafe.
physiatrist_final.public_message: I revise my position. The Deputy Director has correctly pointed to the combination of sphincter dysfunction, progressive myelopathy, and cord compression at C4-C5. These findings, already in the record, signal a high risk of irreversible cord damage if decompression is delayed. Conservative care has no realistic chance of reversing sphincter dysfunction and the patient has already failed 4 months of physiotherapy. I therefore concede that surgical decompression is warranted. My proposed 3-6 month conservative trial is withdrawn. Preoperative evaluation should include high-resolution MRI and CT myelogram to define foraminal and multilevel stenosis and select the optimal approach.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 50-year-old man with progressive cervical compressive myelopathy at C4-C5, evidenced by long tract signs (Babinski, clonus, weakness), sphincter dysfunction, and failed 4 months of physiotherapy. Radiographs indicate a developmentally narrow canal (mid-sagittal diameter 10 mm, Torg ratio 0.37) with superimposed spondylosis at C3-C5. The myelopathy is severe, not mild-to-moderate; further conservative management is not defensible and risks irreversible cord injury. Urgent surgical decompression is indicated, but the optimal approach requires clarification of foraminal involvement, multilevel compression, and cord signal.
proposed_options: Urgent anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) at C4-C5, with possible extension to C3-C6 depending on intraoperative findings and further imaging; foraminal decompression if radicular symptoms correlate.
Posterior cervical decompression (laminectomy/laminoplasty with fusion) if stenosis is multilevel or predominantly dorsal, especially given congenital narrow canal and straight cervical alignment.
Short-interval advanced imaging (high-resolution MRI with T2 and foraminal views, CT myelogram, dynamic radiographs) followed by surgery within days—not a delay for conservative care.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent surgical decompression via ACDF at C4-C5 with intraoperative extension to adjacent levels as needed; preoperative CT myelogram and high-resolution MRI to decide between anterior and posterior approach.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's proposal of a 3–6 month conservative trial. This patient has severe progressive myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction and failed physiotherapy; delaying surgery risks permanent neurological deficit.

Normal patellar and Achilles reflexes despite Babinski and clonus are atypical; this may indicate coexisting peripheral neuropathy or early myelopathy. It merits electrodiagnostic evaluation but does not alter the need for surgery.

Spurling sign and radicular symptoms suggest foraminal stenosis that may require decompression, but the MRI description does not mention foramina. We need dedicated imaging to avoid incomplete surgery.

The radiographs show C3-C5 spurs and a tight canal (10 mm), suggesting multilevel disease. If compression extends beyond C4-C5, anterior-only surgery may be insufficient; a posterior approach should be considered.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that surgery should be scheduled urgently, and should we delay for leukocytosis workup or proceed with a perioperative infectious evaluation?
Would you require a CT myelogram and dynamic radiographs before finalizing the surgical approach?
Given the straight cervical spine and likely multilevel congenital stenosis, do you prefer a posterior decompression over an anterior approach?
How should we formally respond to the physiatrist's request for a time-limited conservative trial? I recommend documenting that it is not indicated.
vice_opinions.public_message: My assessment is severe progressive cervical myelopathy with cord compression at C4-C5 and sphincter dysfunction. I recommend urgent surgical decompression. Further conservative care is not appropriate; the risk of permanent cord injury is too high. Key open questions are the extent of foraminal and multilevel stenosis, and the optimal anterior versus posterior approach. I would obtain a CT myelogram and high-resolution MRI to finalize the plan. I disagree with the proposed 3–6 month conservative trial.

director_rulings.final_decision: Surgery is indicated; obtain high-resolution MRI with dedicated foraminal views, CT myelogram, and dynamic radiographs to finalize surgical approach; reconvene immediately after imaging.
delegated_tasks: Resident to arrange urgent imaging and ensure q4h neurological checks.
director_rulings.reason_for_delay: Need CT myelogram and high-resolution MRI to define foraminal and multilevel stenosis and select optimal surgical approach; imaging is urgent and will be completed within 24 hours.

director_rulings.public_message: Colleagues, I have heard the discussion. Dr. Resident, please give me your specific opinion: given the severe myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, is there any reason to wait for the imaging before taking the patient to the operating room today? Dr. Radiologist, please give me your specific opinion: are the current MRI images sufficient to plan the surgical approach, or do we need further imaging to avoid incomplete decompression? Based on the consensus, surgery is clearly indicated. The physiatrist has withdrawn the conservative trial, and I agree with the deputy that delay risks irreversible cord damage. The neurologist's flags are well taken: the Spurling sign suggests foraminal stenosis not described on the available MRI. Therefore, I rule that we obtain a high-resolution MRI with dedicated foraminal views, a CT myelogram, and dynamic radiographs before finalizing the surgical plan. If imaging confirms isolated C4-C5 compression without significant foraminal stenosis, we will perform ACDF at C4-C5. If imaging reveals multilevel compression or significant foraminal stenosis, we will perform posterior decompression with foraminotomies or an extended anterior procedure. We reconvene as soon as these studies are completed. The patient is to be kept on strict bed rest with neurological checks every 4 hours while awaiting imaging.
